About: Growth and Decay of Current in an LR Circuit

Source

Topic
Electromagnetic Induction — self-inductance and the LR transient
Simulation
One circuit, one clock, one pair of axes. A two-position switch puts the battery in the loop (growth, I = I∞(1 − e−t/τ)) or takes it out and closes a freewheeling loop through R and L alone (decay, I = I₀e−t/τ). Both transients are drawn on the same time axis at the same pixels-per-second, so they are directly comparable.
Concept
An inductor opposes CHANGE in current — not current itself. The steady current is ε/R, set by the resistor alone; L only sets τ = L/R, the time scale of both the rise and the fall.
Inquiry
Predict whether the current jumps to ε/R when the switch closes, and whether it vanishes when the battery is taken out.
Misconception
“Current follows the battery instantly.” It cannot: a step in I would need an infinite dI/dt, and εL = −L·dI/dt would be infinite with it.

CIRCUIT · SWITCH IN POSITION ①
CURRENT vs TIME

Guided Inquiry

1 · The circuit

A battery of EMF ε = 12 V, a resistor R and a coil of inductance L sit in one loop. A two-position switch either puts the battery into that loop (position ①) or takes it out and closes a freewheeling loop through R and L alone (position ②).

Whenever the current changes, the coil sets up a back-EMF εL = −L·dI/dt.

2 · Predict — the switch goes to ①

The switch is thrown to position ① at t = 0. What does the current do?

3 · Predict — double the inductance

Hold R fixed and double L. What happens to the curve?

4 · Predict — the battery is taken out

The switch moves to position ②: the battery leaves, and R and L are left joined in a closed ring. What does the current do?

5 · Predict — what pays for the heat?

In position ② the current still heats the resistor. What supplies that energy?

6 · One sentence

An inductor never opposes current — it opposes change in current. One time constant τ = L/R governs the rise and the fall alike, and the coil's EMF turns round between them: against the battery while the current grows, along the current while it dies.

The Physics

Growth and Decay of Current in an LR Circuit · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A battery, a resistor and a coil share one loop, and a two-position switch decides whether the battery is part of it. The sim draws the current against time as you throw the switch and change the coil and the resistor.

What you'll learn

  • How a coil responds when the current through it is changing.
  • What the time constant τ is, and which parts of the circuit set it.
  • How to read the current-time graph and the live read-outs.
The loop has a battery, a resistor R and a coil L. Contact ① joins the battery to the loop. Contact ② joins the inner rail, which closes a ring of R and L only.

What's on screen

  • Solid curve: the current while the switch is at ①, with a dashed line at the steady current I∞.
  • Dashed curve: the current while the switch is at ②.
  • Read-outs in the side panel: τ, I∞, the live current I, the coil's EMF εL and the resistor drop VR.
  • Moving arrows on the circuit show the path the current takes. They are brighter and faster when I is larger.

03

A coil opposes changes in the current

A current through a coil sets up a magnetic field, and the flux of that field is proportional to the current. If the current changes, the flux changes, and Faraday's law gives the coil an EMF of its own:

εL = −L dI/dt
L is the inductance in henry (H). The minus sign is Lenz's law: εL opposes the change.

Only a change is opposed. While I is steady, εL = 0 and the coil acts like a plain wire. With the battery in the loop, Kirchhoff's loop rule reads VR + VL = ε, where VL = −εL.

Take the instant the switch is thrown to ①. The current is still zero, so VR = 0 and VL = 12 V: εL = −12 V. The current cannot jump, because a step in I would need an infinite dI/dt and an infinite εL.

See itStart a fresh run with the switch at ①, held at t = 0. Watch for: I = 0.000 A and VR = 0.00 V, while εL reads −12.00 V.
04

The current rises along an exponential curve

Put εL into the loop rule, ε − L dI/dt = I R, and solve it starting from I = 0 at t = 0:

I(t) = (ε/R)(1 − e−t/τ)
The steady current is I∞ = ε/R = 12 V / 10 Ω = 1.20 A.

The current starts at zero and climbs steeply while εL is large. It flattens as εL fades. After one time constant τ it has covered 63% of the way to I∞, which is 0.632 × 1.20 A = 0.759 A. After 5τ it is less than 1% short.

At t = τ, εL = −4.42 V and VR = 7.59 V. They still add up to the 12 V of the battery.

See itRun the opening setting, L = 0.10 H and R = 10 Ω, with the switch at ①. Watch for: the marker at τ = 10.0 ms, sitting at 63% of I∞.
05

L sets the speed and R sets the ceiling

The time constant is τ = L/R, in seconds when L is in henry and R in ohm. At L = 0.10 H and R = 10 Ω, τ = 10.0 ms. The ceiling I∞ = ε/R has no L in it, because once I stops changing, εL = 0 and only the resistor limits the current.

Settingτ = L/RI∞ = ε/R
L = 0.10 H, R = 10 Ω10 ms1.20 A
L = 0.20 H, R = 10 Ω20 ms1.20 A
L = 0.10 H, R = 20 Ω5 ms0.60 A

The time axis is fixed at 100 ms, so a larger τ visibly stretches the curve. At ①, the clock stops at 7τ or at 50 ms, whichever comes first. With a large τ the current is still climbing then.

See itDouble L to 0.20 H, keeping R = 10 Ω. Watch for: the dashed ceiling staying at 1.20 A, and the τ marker moving out to 20.0 ms.
See itDouble R to 20 Ω, keeping L = 0.10 H. Watch for: the ceiling dropping to 0.60 A, and the τ marker moving in to 5.0 ms.
06

With the battery out, the current dies away smoothly

At ② the battery is out, and R and L form a closed ring. The loop rule becomes 0 = I R + L dI/dt. Starting from I₀ at the instant of the throw, the solution is:

I(t) = I0 e−t/τ
The same τ = L/R as in the rise. Here I0 is 1.192 A when the switch is thrown at the end of the opening growth.

The current does not stop at once, because that would again need an infinite dI/dt. Instead εL = −L dI/dt turns positive: it now points along the current and keeps it going through R.

One τ after the throw, 37% of I₀ is left: 0.368 × 1.192 A = 0.439 A. The curve is continuous at the throw. It only bends.

See itLet the opening run settle, then the sim throws the switch to ②. Watch for: a dashed curve falling from 1.19 A, with a marker 'one τ later' at about 0.44 A.
07

The energy stored in the coil heats the resistor

A coil carrying current I stores energy in its magnetic field:

U = ½ L I²
At I0 = 1.192 A and L = 0.10 H: U0 = 71.0 mJ.

At ② no battery supplies energy, yet R still heats at the rate I²R. The heat comes from this store. The total heat released in R from the throw onward is exactly U0 = ½ L I0².

U goes as I², so it falls as e−2t/τ. After one τ it is 9.6 mJ, which is 13.5% of U0. While the current grows at ①, the battery pays for both the heat and the energy going into the coil.

See itLet the opening run settle, then the sim throws the switch to ②. Watch for: the stored energy ½LI² falling from 71.0 mJ to about 9.6 mJ one τ later.
08

Where it matters

  • Switching off a coil. The coils in relays, motors and solenoids carry a current that cannot stop at once. If the switch breaks the circuit fast, dI/dt is huge, so εL is huge and can spark across the contacts. A diode placed across the coil gives the current a ring to die away in, which is the situation at ②.
  • Ignition coils. A car's ignition coil builds up a current and then interrupts it quickly. The large εL produced feeds the spark plug.
  • Chokes. A coil placed in a power supply resists sudden changes in current and smooths them out. The time τ = L/R tells you how quickly it can follow.
09

Summary

In one line. In a circuit with a coil, the coil's own EMF governs how the current changes after a switch is thrown, in either position.

Key points

  • εL = −L dI/dt, and τ = L/R.
  • At ①: I = (ε/R)(1 − e−t/τ). At ②: I = I0 e−t/τ.
  • The coil stores U = ½ L I², and that pays for the heat at ②.

Common mix-ups

  • "A bigger coil lowers the final current." L only sets how fast the current gets there. The ceiling ε/R depends on R alone.
  • "A coil opposes current." It opposes a change in current. A steady current meets no opposition from εL.
  • "τ = L × R." It is L divided by R, in seconds. More R means a shorter τ.

Things to try on your own

  • With L = 0.40 H and R = 5 Ω, work out I at 50 ms. The answer is 1.12 A, well short of 2.40 A.
  • With R = 20 Ω, find the L that gives τ = 10 ms. One answer is L = 0.20 H.
  • At the moment of a throw to ②, compare εL with I0R.
